title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Steel Plants | Dye PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection for US steel, aluminum and metals plants: stainless lines, nonferrous parts, castings, weld repairs, bearings. Request a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Steel, Aluminum and Primary Metals Plants in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, finds cracks, laps and porosity open to the surface on any non-porous metal, including the stainless, aluminum and copper alloy parts that magnetic particle testing cannot examine. Atlantis NDT performs PT at US steel mills, foundries, forges and aluminum plants, and technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope. To get started, request a PT inspection quote.

Where penetrant testing belongs in a metals plant

Steel itself is mostly a magnetic particle story, and the page on magnetic particle inspection for steel covers it. Penetrant testing earns its place at the edges: parts that are not magnetic, parts too awkward to magnetize, and welds and castings where a visible, documented surface check is wanted. A metals plant has more of these than people expect. Pickling lines run stainless tanks, piping and fume scrubbers. Aluminum smelters and cast houses use nonferrous tooling and launders. Bearings and bushings are bronze. Hydraulic and lubrication systems have stainless fittings. Even in a carbon steel mill, a part with a rough machined thread or a tight corner may be easier to test with penetrant than with a yoke.

PT can only find what is open to the surface. If the question is what lies inside a section, or how thick a wall has become, ultrasonic testing for steel mills is the right page.

Components and systems where we apply PT

  • Stainless and duplex process equipment. Pickling and acid regeneration lines, scrubbers, heat exchanger shells and tube sheets, welded pipe and tank nozzles. Cracks at welds appear from chloride and thermal cycling.
  • Aluminum components. Cast and fabricated brackets, hoods, frames and handling equipment in smelters and cast houses.
  • Copper alloy and bronze parts. Bearing shells, bushings, wear plates, water-cooled copper elements and electrical bus connections where mechanical cracking is a concern.
  • Machined and ground steel surfaces. Thread roots, keyway corners and small fillets where a yoke does not fit. Grinding cracks from heat treat or abrasive work show well with penetrant.
  • Castings and weld repairs. Surface porosity, shrinkage and hot tears in as-cast or machined castings, and excavations before repair welding.
  • Hydraulic and lubrication hardware. Fittings, manifolds and cylinder components, especially stainless and aluminum parts.

Standards and acceptance

The penetrant method is written up in ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165, with ASTM E1417 covering process controls and materials. For castings, ASTM A903 provides surface acceptance standards for steel castings by magnetic particle and liquid penetrant testing, and weld acceptance is set by AWS D1.1, AWS D14.1 for cranes or the plant's own specification. Where penetrant is used on austenitic stainless or nickel alloys, the code can limit sulfur and halogen content of the penetrant materials, and we use matching qualified materials. The acceptance criteria are chosen by the plant, the engineer or the maker; our report compares each indication to the criterion named in the order. Technicians work under the Atlantis written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II technicians performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. See ASME Section V Article 6 explained for a plain-language guide.

Process control and what changes in a mill setting

  1. Precleaning. The surface must be free of oil, scale, paint and rust. Mills have a lot of all four. We use solvent cleaning, wire brushing or light grinding, and note where grinding is not allowed. Shot-blasting and peening can smear metal over cracks, so those surfaces are sometimes etched before testing.
  2. Penetrant selection. Visible solvent-removable red penetrant is the usual field choice. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and used in a darkened shelter or in the shop.
  3. Dwell time. The penetrant must stay wet on the surface long enough to enter fine cracks. Dwell depends on material, defect type and temperature, and the procedure sets it.
  4. Excess removal. We wipe with clean cloth moistened with solvent, taking care not to wash penetrant out of the defects.
  5. Developer. A thin, even layer of developer draws penetrant out of cracks and gives contrast.
  6. Examination and recording. Indications are read in the specified light within the time window, marked and photographed, and the part is post-cleaned.

Temperature is the main mill problem. Penetrant materials are qualified within a range around roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; a warm roll neck or a freshly welded repair may sit above it. We let the part cool, or, if the code permits, qualify the procedure at the higher temperature. Water-washable systems are avoided around electrical equipment and rarely suit an outage in any case.

What PT finds, and what it does not

Penetrant finds cracks, laps, seams and pores that open to the surface of a clean part, and it works the same on all non-porous alloys. It cannot see closed or buried defects, and a crack that has been smeared shut by grinding, machining or peening can give no indication. Coarse as-cast or blasted surfaces trap penetrant and show a heavy background. We recommend cleaning or light dressing before the test and explain when a part is better examined another way. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and techniques beyond MT, PT and UT are outside this service.

Stainless pickling line weldRight method for surface cracksUT for wall thickness
Aluminum casting or bracketRight methodUT inside for thick sections
Bronze bearing shellRight methodUT for bond

Weld repairs, castings and aluminum cast houses

Three situations produce most of the penetrant work in a metals plant, and each has its own rhythm. The first is repair welding. A cracked bracket, housing or frame is ground or gouged to sound metal, and PT on the excavation shows whether any crack tip remains at the bottom or along the sides of the groove. Leaving a tip behind is the usual reason a repair cracks again, so a clean penetrant result before welding is worth the extra step. The finished weld and the heat-affected zone are examined again once the part reaches the temperature the welding procedure sets for final inspection.

The second is castings. Purchased and in-house castings arrive with surface porosity, shrinkage and hot tears that cannot be seen by eye. PT on the machined faces and critical radii shows them, and the acceptance level depends on the casting specification or the severity class in the purchase order. Gear housings, bearing blocks and pump parts are typical.

The third is aluminum and copper alloy tooling in casting and extrusion operations. Launders, molds, crucible handling frames and extrusion press fixtures run hot and cool repeatedly, so thermal fatigue cracks begin at corners and holes. These parts are non-magnetic and often too complex for a yoke, which makes penetrant the natural method. We examine them at planned changeovers, and the report's photographs let your maintenance team see how a crack has progressed between outages.

Plant access, safety and chemicals

Steel and aluminum plants are tightly managed. Contractors complete safety orientation, follow lock-out and tag-out under 29 CFR 1910.147, obtain confined-space permits under 1910.146 for tanks, scrubbers and ducts, and work under hot work rules where applicable. Penetrant chemicals are flammable solvents, so we agree storage, ventilation and waste handling with the plant, and avoid use in areas where open ignition sources or energized equipment are present. Pickling lines and acid plants often involve extra hazards, and we follow the owner's process isolation steps. Dates are agreed with your planner; we do not promise a crew arrival time.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the component and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant, cleaner and developer with batch numbers, the dwell time, the surface and ambient temperatures, the lighting and the technician and level. Each indication has position, length and shape, with photographs and an accept or reject against the named criterion. Parts are post-cleaned, which is particularly important on stainless and nickel alloys in process service. A Level III reviews and signs the report, and the same format covers re-examination after a repair.

What to send for a quote

  • A list of parts or systems with alloy, thickness, surface finish and operating temperature.
  • Drawings, weld maps or photographs of the areas to be examined.
  • The acceptance code or specification and any limits on penetrant materials.
  • Access arrangements, permits and who supplies power, lighting and lifts.
  • Plant address, safety orientation requirements and the outage window.

Training your plant technicians

Penetrant testing is often the first method a maintenance technician learns, and its quality depends on cleaning and dwell discipline. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training with practice on the penetrant testing simulator. As employer, the plant certifies its technicians under SNT-TC-1A, and written practice development helps put the rules in writing. For the broader picture, read the national penetrant testing page, the comparison of MT versus PT, and the page on manufacturing NDT training. Atlantis's management system is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: When is penetrant testing better than magnetic particle testing on a steel plant?
faq.a: When the material is not magnetic, such as stainless steel, aluminum or bronze, or when the geometry is too tight for a yoke. PT also suits machined corners, thread roots and weld excavations, because the result is visible and easy to document.

faq.q: Can you test parts that are still warm from service?
faq.a: Standard penetrants work in a limited temperature range, so hot parts must cool, or the procedure must be qualified at the higher temperature. We measure surface temperature before starting and record it.

faq.q: Do you use special penetrants on stainless steel pickling lines?
faq.a: Where the specification or plant requires it, we use penetrant materials qualified for low sulfur and halogen content and post-clean the part so no residue remains on process surfaces. The report lists the materials and batch numbers used.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks after grinding or shot peening?
faq.a: Sometimes not, because grinding, machining and peening can smear metal across a crack opening. We etch lightly or choose another method when a smeared surface is likely, and we note the surface condition in the report.

faq.q: Can you work in confined spaces such as scrubbers and tanks?
faq.a: Yes, under the plant's permit program. Penetrant solvents are flammable, so ventilation and ignition control are agreed in advance, and we follow the owner's process isolation steps.

faq.q: What standard governs PT acceptance for castings?
faq.a: ASTM A903 gives surface acceptance standards for steel castings by liquid penetrant and magnetic particle testing, and the purchase specification or owner standard may name stricter limits. We apply whichever criterion your order names.

faq.q: What information do you need to quote penetrant testing?
faq.a: A list of parts with alloys and surface finish, drawings or photographs, the acceptance code, access, permit and utility arrangements, the plant address and the outage window. We reply within one business day to confirm scope.

faq.q: Who decides how a rejected indication is repaired?
faq.a: The plant, the equipment maker or the engineer of record. We report each indication against the named criterion, and repairs, weld procedures and return-to-service decisions are yours. We can re-examine the repair using the same procedure.

faq.q: Can you do X-ray inspection of steel plant welds?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography in the United States is licensed under federal or state radiation rules, and Atlantis does not perform it. Where it is specified, the owner hires a licensed contractor. We can provide ASNT Level III review of the results.
